I hadn't thought of using git to track the changes in legislation. This is a cool idea.
In Australia, I spent a bit of time trying to work out how to find which politician voted for what (both at state and federal level), so that when elections come, you can single out the individuals who voted for what legislation. I think AI may make this easier, but the challenge is in not spamming the "free and open" access to the online record of our legislation.
So far, it's probably a one-person $50K per year job to do this task manually, and the language of the public legislation record didn't lend itself easily to determining the laws or rights that actually changed when bills were passed into legislation. They are explicitly stated, but hard to distill with regexes, filters or other analysis tools (e.g. "Who voted to stop electric scooters going over 25km/h?") If you try reading the legislation, you will know what I mean.
"A complete and open record of the proceedings of our parliament" still needs people spend a good chunk of time interpreting and summarising it (e.g. the media, commentators, etc) which means it's a time-consuming hobby or a paid gig.

I've jokingly said many times that Ghostty GUI is just a glorified tech demo for libghostty. That's not fair though, because GUI is great and there are really talented people working on it.

stories.title_en: Survival LLM: AI assistant and emergency library that runs on your own computer

comments.author: x3haloed
comments.text:
This topic is bringing out the hallucination-panic crowd.
It's perfectly safe to use LLMs to surface underlying data and knowledge without having to trust that it's giving you correct advice.
Use the LLM as search technology: string match -> semantic search -> search intelligence.
This is especially helpful when you don't know the right question to ask. Semantics only help you find text that is semantically near the input query. Semantics won't help you when what you are looking for is connected to what you have by something other than semantics, like causation, mechanism, or interpretation.
Trying to figure out why your crops aren't growing well will likely require you to read several articles across a range of sciences, probably scoped to the specific conditions you are dealing with. A semantic search is not going to surface those first.
Allowing an LLM to chain together several sources for you to read first does not require you to ask it for a conclusion.

stories.title_en: Tailscale SSH: Investigation and remediation update

comments.author: minimaltom
comments.text:
Former tailscalar here and now someone managing tailscale at an org.
Having done my own review of the vulns and the fixes as they are landing in github, its pretty clear to me that this only affects situations where you use ACLs to permit ssh into a node (via tailscale ssh, not via opensshd), but dont give a path to sudoers/root.
If a user had no SSH access and/or connectivity to a vulnerable node, none of these vulns give them access.
However, if you have a vulnerable tailscaled and you give ssh access as some non-root account/privs, then yes, these vulns are relevant as theres now known privilege escalations that give access beyond some specific user account.
Not trying to play down the vuln (its important), but its not a free-for-all RCE that some ppl are acting like it is.

Over the decades, I have maintained remote access through port forwarding on my router - at one point in 2008 I put SSH on port 80 so I could access it from the restricted wifi network at the hospital my grandmother was at. I have also used openvpn. I have also used cloudflare tunnels. But in the end, I always connect to hardened openssh with key only authentication.

stories.title_en: Python's experimental JIT to be removed

comments.author: adrian17
comments.text:
Unfortunate. I've been following the work on it occasionally.
On one hand, it seemed like JIT work was really progressing in high gear until SC requested a new PEP. Also unfortunate, as it seemed like part of the hope for the JIT was that it'd counter the performance penalty from free threading.
On the other, it did feel (to me) like with all the fancy (and definitely cool) optimizations it got (automatic refcount operation removal, new type-based specializations, inplace math operations), the macrobenchmark benefits weren't _that_ exciting for a JIT. It definitely has potential for more, maybe with even fancier optimizations like unboxing ints, but the complexity just keeps going up.
> It said that the PEP was "overly optimistic" about user-visible differences with the JIT enabled.
The JIT is technically generated from the same source as the interpreter loop itself, so originally the differences were extremely unlikely, but I imagine the risk just kept going up as new JIT-only paths and optimizations were introduced.
And politically, I feel like SC’s reasoning was just “this side project has landed in main branch almost by accident and has been stewing without oversight ever since

comments.author: rich_sasha
comments.text:
Here’s an idea instead (maybe it already exists). Allow a decorator for writing inline Cython. It solves, I think, 90% of the problem. On first run, or eagerly, compile the decorated functions. Basically, Cython is the JIT, and user enables it explicitly.
This way I can easily write inlined functions with proper C speed, in a Python esque language.
Reasons why I rarely use Cython without this:
- unmodified Python code running in Cython is often faster, but not that much. 50% or so is my rule of thumb.
- but the development style is very different for Cython and Python, adding a lot of impedance. Eg reloading doesn’t quite work, profiling is different, you need a build directory and a build step at deployment etc.
- Cython proper is different enough and I’d argue unintuitive enough that if I have to have all these things in place, I might as well wrap my function in Rust.
Such a decorator would give you a low friction way to make things faster when you need it, with scope for making it much faster via all the funny Cython, while keeping Python-esque semantics, in particular "development semantics".
I think it would require some language modification since Cython was definitely a sup

https://graalpy.org/python-developers/compatibility/
• They're working on a GIL-free mode
In recent weeks there has been a release of a new web framework for Python that only runs on GraalPy, called Pyronaut (
https://pyronaut.io/

comments.author: FrasiertheLion
comments.text:
We recently wrote about moving away from OVMF (~1M lines of C) to very minimal and hyperspecific firmware (300 lines of assembly)[1] for our specific confidential VM machine targets, and the idea that "popular" does not automatically mean "secure". You can point an LLM at any large codebase and it will find vulnerabilities, so "patch the planet" isn't very scalable. You can instead just write hyperspecific, small codebases and throw all the security practices at it - like LLMs (economical if it's small), fuzzing, formal methods etc.

I've always been downright suspicious of the creation of UEFI. It executes code before the operating system but doesn't really provide a hardware abstraction layer like BIOS does. And unlike BIOS which is relatively small UEFI is "full-fat" almost the size of an operating system itself. It can even run its own applications.
The 1 million lines of C code comprising UEFI are riddled with bugs and this is just one of them. No doubt LLMs will be able to uncover a lot more of them.

stories.title_en: Four Months of Zig

comments.author: i2talics
comments.text:
Why does everyone love being able to control the allocator in Zig? I rarely want this low level control over the allocator, I would rather have an easy to use interface to malloc/free (such as RAII) or would prefer the language push me to avoiding allocations when unnecessary. C and Zig users are always talking about how arena allocators are easier to use than the alternative but I disagree because the alternative is extremely easy to use when the language makes it so.
Arenas have a lot of footguns like growing out of control if you don't have space in your logic to delete them (e.g. suppose every new HTTP connection required obtaining a new allocation from the primary arena -- now you have a memory leak). They also aren't necessarily faster than malloc: I remember hearing a case where mimalloc was
faster
than an arena for a one-shot program like a linker because reclaiming space improved cache locality. Plus it's difficult to implement things like growable vectors or hashmaps using an arena without wasting space.
I just don't see how "futz about with the allocator constantly" and "use an arena" is actually a good default.

comments.author: delifue
comments.text:
The article says some Zig advantages but it's worth noting that all these advantages are tradeoffs.
Zig makes handling error easy but makes retaining error information hard. The result is that Zig developers either write more code than other languages to store diagnostic information, or just simply discard diagnostic information. The second makes it much harder to debug because the useful error information is discarded.
About the TigerStyle, it's worth noting that TigerBeetle doesn't even support variable-sized string type. You can store fixed-sized data, such as a string that's at most 32 bytes. What if the order information contains string longer than 32 bytes? Then you need to store that string in antoher database. TigerBeetle is not a general database. Static memory allocation doesn't fit most applicaitons.
The fallable allocation is useful in embedded system and OS development etc., but useless in common application programming, because OOM results in crash rather than failed allocaiton.
